0006-priestley-new-chart.title: A New Chart of History
0006-priestley-new-chart.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0006-priestley-new-chart.caption: Joseph Priestley’s “A New Chart of History,” created in 1769, inspired by a 1753 chart by Thomas Jefferys. Priestley’s two charts used the same scale so that they could be directly compared. Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0006-priestley-new-chart.altText: An 18th-century timeline by Joseph Priestley dedicated to Benjamin Franklin. The chart spans from around 1200 BCE to the late 1700s CE, with time progressing horizontally. Vertical columns represent different civilizations, empires, and regions.
0006-priestley-new-chart.altTextLong: A complex, grid-like chart that tracks Joseph Priestley’s conception of the history of the world's major empires. The graphic resembles a puzzle, with oddly contoured shapes of muted shades of brown, green, pink, yellow, and, most often, the beige color of the page. On its horizontal X-axis, the chart measures time every hundred years dating all the way back before 1000 B.C. until the time of the chart’s design in 1769. The vertical Y-axis indicates the regions (mostly countries, occasionally continents, like Africa and Asia), over which the empires cataloged in the main body of the graphic had dominion. The most striking, solid block is brown and central to the page: it shows the Roman Empire ruled from 600 B.C. to 400 A.D. across land that is now Italy, Turkey, Spain, Great Britain, and France. Other considerably sized “puzzle pieces” on the chart are the Eastern or Greek Empire, which is to the immediate right of the Roman and also depicted in brown; the Persian Empire in a dark green above and to the left of the Roman block; the Saracens in yellow above and to the right of the Roman Empire; the “Mungl” (Mongol) Empire, pictured above the Saracens, colored in pink; and a conjoined block for the Normans and the English, colored in green. Lining the bottom of the page, above the horizontal timeline, are the names of different monarchs or leaders (beginning with Saul and David, 1,000 B.C. and ending with George III, of the 1760s). In the bottom left-hand corner lies a dedication in elaborate cursive print: “To Benjamin Franklin, L.L.D. F.R.S., this Chart is in Testimony of Esteem and Friendship, Inscribed By his most obliged, Humble Serv! Joseph Priestley.” In small lettering in the top left corner is a brief explanation of the chart, of which the first sentence reads: “This chart is intended to establish a picture of history, or to give a clear view of the rise, progress, extent, and distribution of every considerable empire or state.”
0006-priestley-new-chart.cleanAltText: An 18th-century timeline by Joseph Priestley dedicated to Benjamin Franklin. The chart spans from around 1200 BCE to the late 1700s CE, with time progressing horizontally. Vertical columns represent different civilizations, empires, and regions.

0007-table.title: Table 1.1
0007-table.artist: Stuart Card, Jock Mackinlay, and Ben Shneiderman
0007-table.caption: The hierarchical definition of visualization provided in Stuart Card, Jock Mackinlay, and Ben Shneiderman’s influential visualization textbook, Readings in Information Visualization: Using Vision to Think (Morgan Kaufman, 1999).
0007-table.altText:
A table of definitions describing the layers of cognitive processing and design required for visualization. 

(for html chart):
External Cognition: Use of the external world to accomplish cognition.
Information design: Design of external representations to amplify cognition.
Data graphics: Use of abstract, nonrepresentational visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Visualization: Use of computer-based, interactive visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Scientific visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of scientific data, typically physically based, to amplify cognition.
Information visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of abstract, nonphysically based data to amplify cognition.
0007-table.cleanAltText:
A table of definitions describing the layers of cognitive processing and design required for visualization. 

(for html chart):
External Cognition: Use of the external world to accomplish cognition.
Information design: Design of external representations to amplify cognition.
Data graphics: Use of abstract, nonrepresentational visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Visualization: Use of computer-based, interactive visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Scientific visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of scientific data, typically physically based, to amplify cognition.
Information visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of abstract, nonphysically based data to amplify cognition.
